[[240.8]] 72. DAMARIS LADY MASHAM AN LEIBNIZ

[[240.9]] Oates, 3. (14.) Juni 1704. [67.76.]

[[240.25]] S^#'r Oates 3 June 1704.

[[240.26]] Your great Civilitie Obliges me not the less for haveing presum'd from your Goodness

[[240.27]] upon more than I had any Right to Pretend to when I requested you would give your Self the

[[240.28]] Pains of informing me farther concerning your Hypothesis.

[[240.29]] To a Mind Possess'd in any measure with a Due Admiration of the works of God Nothing

[[240.30]] is more Gratefull than by farther discoveries therein of his Divine Perfections, to be sensibly

[[240.31]] engag'd to Adore that Being which Reason pronounces ought to be the supreme Object of our

[[240.32]] Affections.

[[241.1]] An Hypothesis thought by your self and others conduceing to such an End as this, could

[[241.2]] not but excite my enquirie; and it did so the more because that in reading what you have

[[241.3]] publish'd, it seem'd to my self also you had views there in which gave a very Becomeing Idea

[[241.4]] of the Wisedome of God in his Works. The letter you have favour'd me with confirms me in

[[241.5]] this Thought: but that I may be sure of haveing a certain and cleare knōledge of your

[[241.6]] Hypothesis permit me to tell you what I conceive it to be; in hopes you will rectifie my

[[241.7]] Mistakes if I am in any; which is what may easilie happen to one so little conversant as I am in

[[241.8]] such Speculations.

[[241.9]] You take for granted that there is a Simple Being in us indu'd with Action and

[[241.10]] Perception. The same, you say, differing onely in the manner of Perception, is in

[[241.11]] matter everie where. That that Simple Being in us, which is call'd Soul is distinguish'd

[[241.12]] from that of Beasts (and yet more from that of other Bodys about us) by the Power of

[[241.13]] Abstraction and frameing thereby Universal Ideas. All these Simple Beings you think

[[241.14]] have; Always will have; and ever since they existed have had, Organick Bodys, proportion'd

[[241.15]] to theire Perception. So that not onely after Death the Soul dos remain, but even

[[241.16]] the Animal also. Generation, and Death, being but a displaying or Concealment of these

[[241.17]] Beings to, or from our view. The same Principle of Uniformitie in the Works of Nature which

[[241.18]] has led you to beleeve this has, you say, led you also to your Systeme of the Harmonie

[[241.19]] Preestablish'd betweene Substances. the which I thus understand.

[[241.20]] Any Action of the soul upon Matter, or of Matter upon the Soul is Inconceivable: These

[[241.21]] two have theire Laws distinct. Bodies follow the Laws of Mechanisme, and have a tendencie to

[[241.22]] change suivant les Forces Mouvantes. Souls produce in themselves Internal

[[241.23]] Actions and have a tendencie to change according to the Perception that they have of

[[241.24]] Good or Ill. Now Soul and Body, following each theire Proper Laws, and neither of them

[[241.25]] acting thereby upon, or Affecting the other, such Effects are yet produc'd from a Harmonie

[[241.26]] Preetablish'd betwixt these Substances, as if there was a real communication betweene

[[241.27]] them. So that the Body acting constantly by its owne Laws of Mechanisme without receiving

[[241.28]] any Variation or change therein from any Action of the Soul dos yet always correspond to the

[[241.29]] Passions and Perceptions which the Soul hath. And the Soul, in like Manner, thō not operated

[[241.30]] upon by the Motions of Matter, has yet at the same time that the Body Acts according to its

[[241.31]] Laws of Mechanisme, certain Perceptions or Modifications which fail not to answer thereunto.

[[241.32]] This is what I conceive you to say; in which (to tell you Thoughts so insignificant as mine)

[[241.33]] I see nothing, Peculiar, which seems not possible. I find a Uniformitie in it which pleases me:

[[241.34]] and the Advantages propos'd from this Hypothesis are very desirable. But it appears not yet to

[[241.35]] me that This is more than an Hypothesis; for as Gods ways are not limited by our Conceptions;

[[241.36]] the unintelligibleness or inconceivablness by us of any way but one, dos not, methinks, much

[[242.1]] induce a Beleefe of that, being the way which God has chosen to make use of. Yet such an

[[242.2]] inference as this from our Ignorance, I remember P. Malbranche (or some other assertor of his

[[242.3]] Hypothesis) would make in behalf of Occasional Causes: to which Hypothesis, amongst

[[242.4]] other exceptions, I think there is one, which I cannot, without your help, see, but that yours is

[[242.5]] alike liable to and that is, from the Organization of the Body: wherin all that Nice Curiositie

[[242.6]] that is discoverable seeming Useless: becomes Superfluous and lost labour. To this difficultie

[[242.7]] likewise let me add that I conceive not why Organisme should be, or can be thought, as you

[[242.8]] say is, Essential to Matter.

[[242.9]] But these enquiries, or others, that might it may be on further thoughts occur to me, are

[[242.10]] less pertinent for me to make, than such a one as is more fundamental, althō it dos not

[[242.11]] peculiarly respect your Hypothesis.

[[242.12]] Forms, explain'd by you to signifie Simple Beings, you elsewhere call Atomes des

[[242.13]] Substances, and Forces Primitives, the Nature whereof you, in another place, say, you

[[242.14]] find to Consist in Force.

[[242.15]] Force, I presume cannot be the essence of any Substance, but is the attribute of what you

[[242.16]] call a Form, Soul or Atome de Substance, of the essence whereof I find no positive Idea,

[[242.17]] and your negation of theire haveing any Dimensions, makes theire Existence, I confess,

[[242.18]] inconceivable to me; as not being able to conceive an existence of that which is No Where. If

[[242.19]] the Localitie of these Substances were accounted for by theire being as you [say] they are

[[242.20]] always in Organiz'd Bodies, then they are somewhere: But if these Atomes des Substances

[[242.21]] are somewhere then they must have some extension, which you deny of them: who, I think, also

[[242.22]] place the Union of the Soul with its respective Body in nothing else but that correspondence or

[[242.23]] conformitie whereby, in virtue of a Preestablish'd Harmonie, Souls and Bodys, Acting

[[242.24]] apart, each by theire owne laws, the same effects are produc'd as if theire was a real Communication

[[242.25]] betwixt them. Thō whether, or no, I perfectly comprehend your meaning in this part

[[242.26]] I am in doubt.

[[242.27]] What I have here said I think enough for me to venture to trouble you with at once: and it

[[242.28]] will perhaps be more than enough to show you that you have judg'd by much too favorably of

[[242.29]] my Apprehension. For I remember my Father as well as other Assertors of Unextended

[[242.30]] Substance to have said That it is an imposition of Imagination upon theire Reason in

[[242.31]] Those who cannot be convinc'd of the realitie of substances unextended. So great

[[242.32]] Authoritie as His was to me could not hinder me, if this be so, from being always under such an

[[243.1]] influence of Imagination; which is what would not willingly be in any case. But wherever I

[[243.2]] have no Idea of a thing; or Demonstration of the Truth of any Proposition[,] the Truth of which

[[243.3]] is inconceivable by me, I cannot, and conclude that I ought not to assent to what is asserted of

[[243.4]] either: since should I once do this I know not where I should stop; what should be the

[[243.5]] Boundaries of Assent. Or why I might not Beleeve alike one thing as well as another.

[[243.6]] M^#'r Locke Presents you his humble service, and desires me to tell you He takes himself to

[[243.7]] be mightilie oblig'd to you for your great Civilitie express'd to him; in which he finds you a

[[243.8]] master as well as in Philosophy and every thing else. His want of Health he says now, and the

[[243.9]] little remains he counts he has of Life, has put an end, to his enquiries into Philosophical

[[243.10]] Speculations: thō if he were still in the heat of that Pursuit he could not be so Ignorant of You or

[[243.11]] Himself as to take upon him to be the Judge of what you have well consider'd: much less to be

[[243.12]] the Instructor of a man of your knowne extraordinarie Parts and merit. He takes it for a great

[[243.13]] Honour done him, that you have Condescended to read and consider, as you say, his Essay

[[243.14]] upon the understanding and that you think it worth the while by your Larger Views to

[[243.15]] remove some difficulties, and supply some defects that are therein. This if he had any other end

[[243.16]] in publishing that Treatise but some small service to Truth and Knōledge, would flatter his

[[243.17]] vanitie. That it would be Preserv'd to Posteritie by the touches of so Great a Master: by whose

[[243.18]] Hand it would be redeem'd from some of its own Imperfections.

[[243.19]] All M^#'r Lockes Freinds have at present the greife to apprehend that They shall enjoy the

[[243.20]] Happyness of his Freindship but a little time: the infirmitie of Ill Lungs dayly increaseing upon

[[243.21]] him, in an Age that is considerable.

[[243.22]] I am much Pleas'd S^#'r to have made you a Present, that is both acceptable to you, and that

[[243.23]] can possibly contribute any thing to your inriching the world by the effects of your Meditations.

[[243.24]] If you shall think me Worthy of your Instruction; or at any time of any Communication of your

[[243.25]] Thoughts I shall always (as I ought to do) look upon it as a condescention in you which will

[[243.26]] oblige me to be with the greatest acknowledgment as well as Esteeme

[[243.27]] S^#'r Your Most Humble Servant Da Masham.
